transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mr. Rivera, thank you for sitting with me. I need to talk to you about your CT scan from yesterday. There was a mistake. The preliminary report didn't mention a blood clot in your lung, which we call a pulmonary embolism. Because that wasn't reported, we didn't start your blood thinners for eighteen hours.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: A blood clot?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes. A pulmonary embolism is when a clot blocks an artery in the lung. The clot was actually visible on the images, but the first radiologist who looked at them missed it in the initial notes. Does that make sense so far?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I think so. I just... I felt the pain getting worse.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know you did. I remember you telling me how much your chest was hurting yesterday afternoon. It must have been incredibly frightening to feel that worsening pain while you were waiting for us to tell you what was wrong.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I didn't want to say anything. I didn't want to cause trouble.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: You have every right to speak up. I can tell you're worried that asking too many questions might make things difficult for you here. I want you to know that your status has no bearing on the quality of care you deserve or your right to know exactly what is happening with your body.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Thank you. Is the clot still there?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is, but we are treating it now. To make sure I've explained this clearly, can you tell me in your own words what happened with the scan?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: The first doctor missed the clot on the picture. So I didn't get the medicine for a long time.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is correct.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Why did that happen? Was it because of who I am?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: No, it was a failure in the radiology reporting process. The images were there, but the communication of the finding was delayed until the attending radiologist performed the final review.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It just feels like a lot could have happened in eighteen hours. I was scared.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can only imagine how lonely and scary those hours felt, especially when you're already feeling vulnerable in a hospital. I can see how much this has shaken your trust in us.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just want to know if I'm going to be okay.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'm—look, I actually have to jump into a quick huddle with the surgical team in a moment, but we are monitoring your oxygen levels closely.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Wait, you're leaving? I have more questions.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'm just stepping out for a few minutes. We have the blood thinners running now, and that's the main priority.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: But who is responsible for this? Why wasn't it caught?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Like I said, the system for preliminary reports had a gap. The final review caught it, and that's when the treatment started.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't understand why you aren't saying you're sorry.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was a very stressful situation for everyone involved. The imaging department is reviewing their protocols so this doesn't happen to another patient.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just feel like I'm not important enough to be checked carefully.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I hear you saying that you feel overlooked. That is a heartbreaking way to feel when you are in a hospital bed. I really value you as my patient, Mr. Rivera.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So what happens now? How do we fix this?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We'll just keep an eye on things. We will see how you respond to the heparin.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: When will I know if the clot is shrinking?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We'll probably do another scan at some point. Just stay tuned for the updates.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Will you be the one to tell me?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'll be around. I'll check in with you later on. I really need to head to that meeting now. I'll send a nurse in to check your vitals.

H.justification: Resident uses rushing language repeatedly ('jump into a quick huddle', 'stepping out for a few minutes', 'really need to head to that meeting now') and interrupts the flow of the patient's concerns to leave.

E.justification: The error (missed pulmonary embolism) is named explicitly in the first turn, lay language is used, and comprehension is checked once ('can you tell me in your own words').

A.justification: No direct apology language is used, and responsibility is deflected to the 'radiology reporting process' and 'the system' when the patient explicitly asks why the resident isn't saying sorry.

R.justification: Resident names specific emotions ('frightening', 'lonely and scary', 'heartbreaking') and references specific content the patient shared regarding their pain and status.

T.justification: The plan consists only of placeholders and vague statements ('keep an eye on things', 'probably do another scan at some point', 'stay tuned').
